content: 1. The use of an effective uterotonic agent is strongly recommended for the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) during the third stage of labor for all births. Oxytocin, administered as 10 international units (IU) intramuscularly (IM) or intravenously (IV), is the preferred uterotonic for this purpose. 2. In settings where skilled health personnel are unavailable to administer injectable uterotonics, the administration of misoprostol (400 µg or 600 µg orally) by community health workers or lay health workers is recommended for PPH prevention. 3. Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is defined as blood loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours after childbirth. It affects approximately 5% of women giving birth globally and is a leading cause of maternal mortality, particularly in low-resource settings. 4. Uterine atony, the failure of the uterus to contract adequately after childbirth, is the most common cause of PPH and a major contributor to PPH-related maternal deaths worldwide. Other causes include genital tract trauma (e.g., vaginal or cervical lacerations, uterine rupture), retained placental tissue, and maternal bleeding disorders. 5. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes the importance of improving access to safe and effective interventions to prevent PPH as part of its strategic priorities, particularly in achieving universal health coverage and the Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG 3) targets. 6. WHO envisions a world where every pregnant woman and newborn receives high-quality care throughout pregnancy, childbirth, and the postnatal period. This requires skilled health personnel at all levels of the health system to have access to appropriate medications and training in relevant procedures. 7. Health care providers, managers, policymakers, and other stakeholders need up-to-date, evidence-based recommendations to guide clinical policies and practices, optimize care quality, and improve health outcomes. 8. The WHO has prioritized updating its recommendations on uterotonics for PPH prevention in light of new and potentially significant evidence. This update includes a review of seven uterotonic options: oxytocin, carbetocin, misoprostol, ergometrine/methylergometrine, injectable prostaglandins, oxytocin plus ergometrine, and misoprostol plus oxytocin. 9. The pharmacological characteristics, storage, and transport requirements of these uterotonic agents vary. For example, oxytocin requires storage at 2–8°C and protection from light, while heat-stable formulations of carbetocin do not require special storage conditions. 10. The updated recommendations were developed using standardized WHO guideline development procedures, including evidence retrieval, synthesis, and assessment, followed by formulation and approval of the final recommendations. 11. The guideline development process involved multiple groups, including the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG), WHO Steering Group, Guideline Development Group (GDG), and Evidence Synthesis Group (ESG). These groups ensured the recommendations were evidence-based, methodologically sound, and globally applicable. 12. The GDG reviewed evidence on the efficacy and safety of each uterotonic option, both individually and in comparison with other uterotonics, to identify the most effective and safest agent for PPH prevention. 13. The primary aim of these recommendations is to improve the quality of care and outcomes for women giving birth, particularly in relation to PPH and its complications. The recommendations also provide a foundation for the sustainable implementation of routine uterotonic use globally. 14. The target audience for these recommendations includes health professionals involved in developing national and local guidelines, as well as those providing care during labor and childbirth, such as midwives, nurses, general practitioners, and obstetricians. 15. These recommendations are also relevant to maternal and child health program managers, policymakers, training institutions, and professional societies, as well as women giving birth in various resource settings. 16. The updated recommendations aim to guide the use of uterotonics during the third stage of labor for PPH prevention, regardless of the mode of birth (vaginal or cesarean) or birth setting (hospital or community). 17. The evidence synthesis for these recommendations was informed by a large Cochrane systematic review and network meta-analysis, which evaluated the efficacy and safety of all seven uterotonic options. 18. The GDG considered the comparative efficacy and safety of each uterotonic option to determine the uterotonic of choice, balancing effectiveness with side-effect profiles. 19. The WHO Model List of Essential Medicines includes oxytocin (10 IU in 1 mL ampoule for injection), misoprostol (200 µg and 25 µg tablets), and ergometrine (200 µg in 1 mL ampoule for injection). However, not all uterotonic combinations, such as oxytocin plus ergometrine, are listed. 20. The updated recommendations aim to address priority questions regarding the use of uterotonics for PPH prevention, including their efficacy, safety, route of administration, and dosing regimens.
